newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan says Indian jet intruder reconnoitring.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says Indian jet intruder reconnoitring.

text.p: Pakistan Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told parliament on Thursday an Indian air force jet fighter alleged to have intruded into Pakistani airspace on Tuesday seemed to be on a spying mission.
"One can safely say that the aircraft was on a reconnaissance mission," he said in the Senate (upper house) in response to a point of order raised by an opposition Senator.
Khan said the violation was apparently meant to test Pakistan's radar system.
India on Thursday denied that one of its jet fighters had violated Pakistan's airspace and said the sonic boom that shook Islamabad could have been produced by a plane outside Pakistan's borders.

The Pakistan Air Force (PAF) said on Wednesday a loud boom that rattled windows of buildings in Islamabad on Tuesday was caused by an Indian jet when it broke the sound barrier while flying out of Pakistani airspace.
Pakistan on Wednesday lodged a strong protest with India, saying the suspected intrusion violated international law and a bilateral agreement.
But New Delhi said no Indian aircraft had crossed the border. "We deny any Indian aircraft, either civilian or military, crossed the international border," a Defence Ministry spokesman said.

Khan said an Indian jet that carried out a similar intrusion in 1959 was shot down, but he added that Pakistan did not have a missile system to deter intrusion at the height taken by the Indian jet, which the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) said was more than 60,000 feet (18,288 metres).
However, he said: "We have to take precautionary measures."
A Foreign Ministry spokesman said earlier that there were two intrusions into Pakistani airspace on Tuesday, probably by the same plane.
The Indian spokesman said a sonic boom can be heard from as far away as 120 km (75 miles), depending on the aircraft's speed, altitude and direction.
Islamabad is about 80 km (50 miles) from the line of control dividing Pakistan and the Indian region of Jammu.
"If a sonic boom occurs on this side of the border, it may be heard on the other side," the Indian Defence Ministry spokesman said.
The spokesman, however, said he knew of no plane that broke the sonic boom in Indian airspace on Tuesday.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, the last one in 1971, but recently resumed bilateral talks to normalise relations.
